svg.text: Lifelong treatment for a disease that never hurts
Every reason a patient stops is rational from where she is standing. Argue with the reason, not the patient.
What she says, and what it means
"I felt well, so I stopped."
Nobody explained that it never causes symptoms.
"The tablets finished and money was short."
A cost problem, not a motivation problem.
"They made me pass urine all night."
A real side effect with a real solution: change the timing.
Each has a different remedy. Guessing wastes the visit.
How to ask so you get the truth
Not: "Are you taking your tablets?"
That question has only one socially safe answer.
Instead: "Many people find it hard to take
these every day. How many days last week
did you miss?"
Normalising it first, then asking for a number,
gives you something far closer to the truth.
The advice that actually gets followed in a Ghanaian household
Not "reduce salt" but: cook without the shrimp powder and the stock cubes, and taste before you add anything.
Not "take more exercise" but: walk to the market instead of taking the taxi, four days a week.
Name the food. Name the day. Vague advice is advice nobody can act on.
The conversation that decides whether she comes back
Blame guarantees she will say yes next time whether or not it is true, and eventually that she stops attending at all.
A patient who can admit missing doses without being scolded is a patient whose treatment you can actually fix.
Non-adherence is a problem to be diagnosed, exactly like breathlessness or pain.
